supplement.holds: No supplementary material or appendix is referenced or included in the complete PDF. Section 3.6 (PDF p. 8, journal p. 86) describes t-tests, ANCOVA and Cohen's d, but the writing results (PDF pp. 11-12, journal pp. 89-90) supply no corresponding numerical test results or control-group means.

paper_design_summary: At a Hong Kong secondary school, 76 Form 4 and Form 5 students were assigned to a five-week, ten-hour GenAI storytelling workshop or conventional English lessons without AI, with 38 assigned per group (PDF p. 5, Section 3.1). The abstract claims random assignment, while Section 3.3 also calls the design quasi-experimental; actual randomization, the allocation unit, and the number of people analyzed remain unconfirmed (PDF pp. 1, 6 and 8). Both groups received storytelling tests without AI immediately before and after the intervention, and writing samples were assessed for word usage, narrative structure, creativity and total writing score; the assessors and analysis unit are not identified (PDF p. 6, Figure 1 and Section 3.3; p. 8, Sections 3.3.1 and 3.6; pp. 11-12, RQ3 and Figure 3).

studies.label: School GenAI storytelling workshop versus conventional English lessons

assignment.what_was_assigned: GenAI storytelling workshop versus conventional English lessons without AI. The abstract explicitly claims random assignment, and Section 3.3 describes assignment through simple random sampling, but that same section labels the design quasi-experimental. The source does not resolve these conflicting descriptions; randomized and design_class are null pending clarification of the allocation procedure and unit.
assignment.quote: Participants were assigned to either the experimental or control group through a process of simple random sampling.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 6 (journal p. 84), Section 3.3, first and final sentences; PDF p. 1 (journal p. 79), abstract. The random-assignment claim and quasi-experimental label conflict; no further allocation details or explicit allocation unit are given.
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration statement in the complete document, PDF pp. 1-17.

arms.name: Experimental group (GenAI storytelling workshop)
arms.description: Five consecutive weeks with two 60-minute sessions per week, ten hours in total, in the school computer lab; instruction covered AI concepts, text prompting and outlining, visuals, music, and story editing/presentation, with instructor-designed prompt banks and guided examples (PDF pp. 5-7, Sections 3.1-3.2 and Table 1). The 38 in n_randomized is the reported assignment count; randomization is unconfirmed and the analyzed count is not stated (PDF pp. 1, 5-6 and 8, abstract, Sections 3.1, 3.3 and 4.1, and Figure 1).

arms.name: Control group (conventional English lessons)
arms.description: Conventional English lessons without exposure to AI tools (PDF p. 5, Section 3.1). The 38 in n_randomized is the reported assignment count; randomization is unconfirmed and the analyzed count is not stated (PDF pp. 1, 5-6 and 8, abstract, Sections 3.1, 3.3 and 4.1, and Figure 1).

participants.exclusions: No exclusions or attrition are reported, but no explicit post-test or analyzed participant count is given. The 76 students and 38 per group refer to assignment; the Results section repeats that students were divided into groups and does not establish the analysis denominator (PDF p. 5, Section 3.1; p. 6, Figure 1; p. 8, Section 4.1). The n_randomized fields retain the paper's reported assignment counts only; the conflicting design descriptions leave actual randomization unconfirmed.
participants.who: Form 4 and Form 5 students at a government-funded Band 3 secondary school in a public housing district serving socioeconomically disadvantaged students, with limited digital resources and low digital/GenAI literacy. The experimental group included 18 Form 4 and 20 Form 5 students (PDF p. 5, Section 3.1; p. 8, Section 4.1).
participants.quote: This study was conducted at a Band 3 secondary school in Hong Kong and involved a total of 76 students from Form 4 and Form 5.
participants.locator: PDF p. 5 (journal p. 83), Section 3.1; PDF p. 6 (journal p. 84), Figure 1; PDF p. 8 (journal p. 86), Section 4.1. None provides an explicit analyzed count.

ai_tool.how_used: Unnamed generative tools supported brainstorming, prompt crafting and outlining, visual creation/revision, and AI music during a guided multimodal storytelling workshop; final activities included story editing, peer review and presentation. Instructor-designed prompt banks and guided examples supported use. Neither a product nor a model/version is identified for the intervention (PDF pp. 6-7, Section 3.2 and Table 1). The scored storytelling tests used no AI help (PDF p. 6, Figure 1).

task.description: Storytelling tests without AI at pre-test and post-test (PDF p. 6, Figure 1). Writing samples were assessed using the Carey et al. (2022) Creative Writing Assessment Rubric on word usage, narrative structure and creativity (PDF p. 8, Section 3.3.1); the total writing score was out of 15 (PDF p. 11, RQ3). Exact prompts and per-dimension scoring anchors are not given.
task.duration: Test duration not stated. The intervention lasted five weeks with two 60-minute sessions per week, ten hours in total (PDF p. 5, Sections 3.1-3.2).

outcomes.name: Creativity of the unassisted post-test story
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Creativity dimension from the Creative Writing Assessment Rubric (Carey et al., 2022; PDF p. 8, Section 3.3.1; PDF pp. 11-12, RQ3 and Figure 3). The scorer's identity and type, blinding and reliability are not reported; expert or lay human ratings cannot be confirmed, so measure is null. The paper does not reproduce the rubric's per-dimension score range or anchors. The number of writing samples per student, any aggregation of sample or rater scores, and the observation used in the writing analysis are not specified, so unit and n_units are null (PDF p. 8, Sections 3.3.1(c) and 3.6; PDF pp. 11-12, RQ3 and Figure 3).
outcomes.delay: Post-test immediately after the five-week intervention; no later follow-up is reported (PDF p. 6, Section 3.3 and Figure 1).

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is unclear: the abstract explicitly claims random assignment (PDF p. 1), and Section 3.3 describes assignment through simple random sampling, but that same section labels the study quasi-experimental and provides no further allocation details or explicit assignment unit (PDF p. 6). Neither random nor nonrandom assignment is confirmed; assignment.randomized and design_class are null. Criterion 2 is unclear: 76 students were assigned, 38 per arm (PDF p. 5, Section 3.1; p. 6, Figure 1), but no quantitative analyzed count is reported. The grouping count in Results (PDF p. 8, Section 4.1) does not establish at least 50 people analyzed. Criterion 3 is met: the Creative Writing Assessment Rubric scores creativity on students' writing samples (PDF p. 8, Section 3.3.1(c); PDF pp. 11-12, RQ3 and Figure 3). The unidentified scorer and analysis unit do not change this output-scoring finding. Figure 1 labels both storytelling tests as No AI Help (PDF p. 6), so the outcomes are after_ai. No numerical between-group writing estimate is printed (PDF pp. 11-12).

one_line_finding: After a five-week GenAI workshop, the experimental group's no-AI writing mean rose from 3.34 to 8.71 out of 15, with reported creativity gains but no numerical between-group writing result (PDF pp. 11-12, RQ3 and Figure 3).
open_questions: What allocation procedure and unit were used, and how is the random-assignment claim reconciled with the quasi-experimental label?
How many students completed each writing test and entered each writing analysis, overall and by arm?
Who or what scored the writing samples, and what were the raters' expertise, blinding, reliability and per-dimension scoring anchors?
What were the exact writing-dimension means, SDs and analyzed counts, and the control-group means and between-group ANCOVA or other results?
Which generative AI products and model versions were used in the workshop?
What was one observation in each writing analysis, how many writing samples did each student contribute at each testing point, and how were any multiple sample or rater scores aggregated?
notes: Final review covered all 418 markdown lines, including references and the author biography; the 17-page PDF has no appendix or referenced supplement. Eligibility passages and recorded numerical results were checked with PyMuPDF text extraction, Table 1 with find_tables, and all four raster figures in memory. The assignment and outcome challenges each identify one correctable coding problem; the people challenge lists no problems. The assignment correction removes affirmative randomized/design codes while retaining the paper's explicit random-assignment claim and reported assignment counts. The outcome correction sets all four analysis units to null because an observation in the analysis is not defined. These are two corrected challenge problems; the underlying methodological omissions remain in final.open_items. The reconciliation object is unchanged historical documentation; final fields supersede its provisional codes. All four output-scored outcomes are retained. Word usage and narrative structure are usefulness under the codebook's output-quality definition, and total writing score is other because it combines those dimensions with creativity. The scorer is unidentified, so measure remains null. No diversity or AI-available performance outcome is reported. AI-literacy and writing-anxiety questionnaires and qualitative interviews are excluded from the output-scored inventory. Figure 1 identifies nine interviews as a qualitative subset; these are not additional participants or a quantitative analyzed denominator (PDF p. 6, Figure 1; p. 8, Section 3.3.2). The 76 and 38-per-arm counts are reported at assignment, not after exclusions; attrition and quantitative analyzed counts are unreported. Experimental-group total writing means of 3.34 and 8.71 out of 15 are printed in prose (PDF p. 11, RQ3). The statistics_available array for that contrast remains empty because the permitted vocabulary has no means-only category. No dimension means are estimated from Figure 3 bar heights; the reconciliation retains prior guesses solely as historical disagreement records. Significant within-group change in one arm and nonsignificant change in the other do not establish a between-group effect, so between-group directions remain null. The workshop comparison combines GenAI exposure with a different instructional program (PDF p. 5, Section 3.1). The printed p < .001 on PDF p. 11 concerns writing anxiety, not the scored writing dimensions. Missing scoring details, analysis units, effect statistics and model names do not independently defeat the three eligibility criteria; the allocation conflict and missing analyzed people count prevent a core inclusion decision.

challenge_resolution.problem: studies[0].assignment.randomized=yes and design_class=field_rct encode confirmed randomization despite conflicting design descriptions.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: Set assignment.randomized and design_class to null and revised the assignment description and eligibility reason. The abstract's random-assignment claim and Section 3.3's simple-random-sampling statement are preserved alongside the quasi-experimental label. Reported assignment counts remain 76 overall and 38 per arm, explicitly qualified as assignment counts with unconfirmed randomization. The source does not establish nonrandom assignment either. Criterion 1 remains unclear pending author clarification.
challenge_resolution.quote: The study employed a pretest-posttest quasi-experimental design (see Figure 1) and adopted a mixed-methods research approach.
challenge_resolution.locator: PDF p. 6 (journal p. 84), Section 3.3, first and final sentences; contrasting random-assignment claim on PDF p. 1 (journal p. 79), abstract; assignment counts on PDF p. 5, Section 3.1, and p. 6, Figure 1.

challenge_resolution.problem: The participant analysis unit for outcomes S1-O1, S1-O2, S1-O3 and S1-O4 is not explicitly supported.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: Changed unit from participant to null for all four writing outcomes, documented the missing observation and score-aggregation details, and added an open question. Paired t-tests and ANCOVA are named, but the paper does not specify the number of samples per student or how sample or rater scores entered an analysis. Criterion 3 remains met because creativity is explicitly assessed on writing samples.
challenge_resolution.quote: Within-group changes from pre- to post-test were examined using paired samples t-tests.
challenge_resolution.locator: PDF p. 8 (journal p. 86), Sections 3.3.1(c) and 3.6; PDF p. 11 (journal p. 89), RQ3; PDF p. 12 (journal p. 90), Figure 3. No additional analysis-unit description in the complete document.

open_items.item: Allocation procedure and unit, including the random-assignment/quasi-experimental conflict (open question 1; unresolved reconciliation assignment.unit, criterion_1_random_assignment_of_ai, and the assignment component of eligibility.core). This affects criterion 1. An author description of how the groups were allocated and at what unit would settle it (PDF pp. 1 and 6, abstract and Section 3.3).

People analyzed for each writing outcome, overall and by arm, including post-test completion, exclusions and missing data (open question 2 and the analyzed-count component of open question 4; unresolved reconciliation participants.n_analyzed and the count component of eligibility.core). This affects criterion 2. Author-supplied participant-flow and analysis counts would establish whether at least 50 people were analyzed; the reported 76 and 38 per arm are assignment counts (PDF pp. 5-6, 8 and 11-12, Sections 3.1, 3.3 and 4.1, RQ3 and Figures 1 and 3).

Scorer identity/type, expertise, blinding, reliability and scoring anchors (open question 3; all four unresolved reconciliation outcomes[0-3].measure differences, S1-O1 through S1-O4). Author-supplied scoring documentation would settle these details. No eligibility criterion depends on which permitted scorer type was used; output-scored creativity is already explicit (PDF p. 8, Section 3.3.1(c)).

Exact writing-dimension means, SDs, control-group means and between-group ANCOVA or other results (the effect-statistics component of open question 4). Author-supplied result tables would settle these omissions (PDF p. 8, Section 3.6; pp. 11-12, RQ3 and Figure 3). These affect effect extraction, not the three eligibility criteria; the analyzed-count component is assessed separately above.

Names and versions of the generative AI products used (open question 5). An author-supplied intervention-tool list would settle this. No eligibility criterion is affected because generative text, image and music assistance is established by the activities (PDF pp. 6-7, Section 3.2 and Table 1).

Analysis unit, writing samples per student and aggregation of sample or rater scores for S1-O1 through S1-O4 (new open question 6 and outcome challenge). Author-supplied scoring and analysis documentation would settle this (PDF p. 8, Sections 3.3.1(c) and 3.6; pp. 11-12, RQ3 and Figure 3). This affects extraction and uncertainty assessment; the output-scoring criterion is met and the eligibility-critical analyzed people count is tracked separately.
